items.title: Frank Chace Interview, 1961-11-18
items.q: When I was first learning how to play, I bought a clarinet from McCracken. I was very young, and I asked him what he thought of Pee-wee Russell

ctx.x: The clarinetist who left Chicago and has joined those West Coast boys. Bob McCracken? McCracken, for one. I don't hear anything particularly derivative in Bob, nor anything particularly characteristic. Am I right about that? I think so.

When I was first learning how to play, I bought a clarinet from McCracken. I was very young, and I asked him what he thought of Pee-wee Russell, and he demurred for a moment, and then he said, well, Pee-wee's a stylist. And then either said nothing or talked about something else. McCracken, I guess, is, as far as I know, an extremely accomplished clarinet player, but my opinion is that there are thousands like that, and it's awfully hard to try to figure out what connection they have with traditional jazz. I…

They learned the tunes, and they may have shaped the tune a little in terms of what they heard somebody else play, but retained an indifference rather than developed a personality or developed a copy style.
